passages.happening:
The angel of the LORD goes up from Gilgal to a place called Bochim and speaks in God's own voice: “I brought you up out of Egypt and led you into the land that I had promised to your fathers” (verse 1). God had promised never to break his covenant with them. He had asked only that they make no covenant with the people of the land and that they tear down their altars. “Yet you have not obeyed My voice. What is this you have done?” (verse 2).

So God says he will no longer drive those peoples out: “they will be thorns in your sides, and their gods will be a snare to you” (verse 3).

When the people hear it, they weep aloud. The place is named Bochim, and they offer sacrifices there to the LORD (verses 4-5).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 1 told the story of the unfinished conquest from the outside, tribe by tribe. This scene tells it from God's side. What looked like bad luck in war is called by its true name: disobedience.

Gilgal was Israel's first camp after crossing the Jordan, the place where twelve stones from the river had been set up and the covenant sign renewed. It was a place of memory. The messenger comes from there, as if bringing Israel's own beginning to stand in front of it. Bochim is not otherwise known. The ancient Greek translation links it with Bethel, which was nearby. Its name means weepers, and it is given because of what happened there.

The angel speaks as God himself: ‘I brought you up out of Egypt’. That is why the angel of the LORD has puzzled readers. The question of who he is comes up again with Gideon and with Samson's parents, and the hard question below sets out the main answers.

The charge is precise. Israel was not told to love Canaanite religion less. It was told not to make covenants with the people of the land and to tear down their altars, because those altars would pull Israel's heart away. Israel did neither. ‘What is this you have done?’ is the very question God put to the woman in the garden (Genesis 3:13). It asks for a confession.

The people weep, and they offer sacrifice. That is not nothing. But the rest of the chapter, and the rest of the book, will show that tears at Bochim did not change what Israel did next.
passages.later:
The warning had been given before. Moses spoke of the peoples left in the land as ‘barbs in your eyes and thorns in your sides’ (Numbers 33:55), and Joshua repeated it at the end of his life: “they will become for you a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes” (Joshua 23:13).

Paul names the difference between sorrow that changes a person and sorrow that does not: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
passages.hard:
Who is the angel of the LORD, who speaks here as God himself?

He says ‘I brought you up out of Egypt’, and he speaks of ‘My covenant’. Readers have answered the question of who he is in more than one way.

Many Christian interpreters, from the early church on, have seen him as an appearance of God the Son before he was born as a man. Others read him as a created messenger who carries God's name and speaks with God's full authority, so that to hear him is to hear God.

These notes do not choose between these readings. What is not in doubt is the message. The God who rescued Israel from Egypt is the one now holding Israel to account.
passages.asks: God's question was ‘What is this you have done?’ Ask what you would answer if he asked it of you today, plainly and without excuses. And think about the tears at Bochim. Ask whether your sorrow over a wrong has ever stopped at tears, and what it would take for it to change what you do tomorrow.

passages.t: A generation that did not know the LORD
passages.happening:
The writer steps back to Joshua's last days. Joshua sends the people home, each tribe to its own land (verse 6). “And the people served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him, who had seen all the great works that the LORD had done for Israel” (verse 7).

Joshua dies at the age of 110 and is buried in his own land, in the hill country of Ephraim (verses 8-9).

Then comes the sentence on which the whole book turns. “After that whole generation had also been gathered to their fathers, another generation rose up who did not know the LORD or the works that He had done for Israel” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
These verses repeat, almost word for word, the last lines of the book of Joshua. The repetition marks a change of generation. One age is closing, and another is beginning.

The generation that served the LORD is described carefully. They ‘had seen all the great works’ God had done: the crossing of the Jordan, the fall of Jericho, the land given. Their faith rested on what they had seen.

‘Gathered to their fathers’ was a way of speaking of death and burial with one's family.

The word ‘know’ in verse 10 means more than having information. In Hebrew it often means knowing by experience, as a person knows a friend. The new generation may well have heard the stories. They did not know the God in them. Faith had not been passed on.

The law had told parents exactly how to pass it on, in ordinary talk at home and on the road, morning and night. It had also warned that comfort would be the danger: when Israel was settled in houses it had not built, eating from vines it had not planted, it would be tempted to forget. That is what happened. No enemy stole this generation's faith. It was simply not handed down.

Joshua's burial place is called Timnath-heres here and Timnath-serah in the book of Joshua. The two names have the same letters in a different order. Some scholars think one form was changed on purpose, since heres is a word for the sun. Others see a simple copying difference. The place is the same.
passages.later:
The book of Joshua ends with nearly the same lines: “Israel had served the LORD throughout the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and who had experienced all the works that the LORD had done for Israel” (Joshua 24:31).

The law had said how faith was to be passed on: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up” (Deuteronomy 6:7). It also named the danger of plenty: “be careful not to forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Deuteronomy 6:12).

A psalm says that God gave his law and told the fathers to teach it to their children, “that the coming generation would know them” (Psalm 78:6). Judges tells what happened when that teaching failed.
passages.asks: The new generation had heard of God, but they did not know him. Ask whether your own faith rests on what you have seen God do, or only on what you have been told. If you have children or others in your care, ask whether they hear you speak of God at home and on the road, or only in church. And ask what you are doing to make sure the next generation knows not only the stories but the God in them.

passages.t: The pattern of the whole book
passages.happening:
Now the writer sets out in a few verses what the rest of the book will show again and again.

‘And the Israelites did evil in the sight of the LORD and served the Baals’ (verse 11). They leave the God who brought them out of Egypt and follow the gods of the peoples around them, Baal and the Ashtoreths (verses 12-13).

So the anger of the LORD burns. He gives them into the hands of raiders and of their enemies all around, and they can no longer stand against them. Wherever they march out, the hand of the LORD is against them, as he had warned. ‘So they were greatly distressed’ (verses 14-15).

“Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them from the hands of those who plundered them” (verse 16). But they will not listen even to their judges, and they quickly turn away (verse 17). While a judge lives, God is with that judge and saves them, “for the LORD was moved to pity by their groaning under those who oppressed them and afflicted them” (verse 18).

“But when the judge died, the Israelites became even more corrupt than their fathers, going after other gods to serve them and bow down to them” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
This is the key to the middle of the book. Every story from Othniel to Samson is another turn of this wheel: Israel does evil, God hands them over, they are in distress, God raises up a judge, the judge saves them, the judge dies, and they fall again. Later stories add a step that is only hinted at here: the people cry out to God, and he hears them.

But the wheel does not just turn. It runs downhill. Verse 19 says each generation became ‘even more corrupt than their fathers’. The book traces a spiral going down, and it ends somewhere worse than where it began.

Baal was the great god of the Canaanites, the storm god believed to bring the rain, and with it the crops, the flocks and children. Texts found at Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, in the late 1920s tell of his battles, his death and his return to life, which his worshipers tied to the dry and rainy seasons. ‘The Baals’ probably means the many local forms of the god, each with its own shrine. The Ashtoreths were forms of Astarte, a goddess of fertility and war. For farmers who lived or died by the rain, these gods seemed a practical safeguard. Serving them did not feel like leaving the LORD. It felt like good farming.

The Hebrew word for judge in verse 16 is shophet. It does not mainly mean someone who sits in a court. It means someone who puts things right, and in this book the judges are chiefly deliverers whom God raised up to free Israel and then to lead it. The verb ‘saved’ in verse 16 comes from the same root as the names Joshua and Jesus.

Notice verse 18. The LORD was moved to pity by their groaning. The verse does not say they had turned back to him first. His mercy is what keeps the wheel from ending in Israel's destruction.
passages.later:
Israel itself later read its history this way. The prayer in Nehemiah remembers it: “So You delivered them into the hands of enemies who oppressed them, and in their time of distress they cried out to You. From heaven You heard them, and in Your great compassion You gave them deliverers who saved them from the hands of their enemies” (Nehemiah 9:27).

A psalm holds the same two things together, the repeated sin and the patient God: “Many times He rescued them, but they were bent on rebellion and sank down in their iniquity. Nevertheless He heard their cry; He took note of their distress” (Psalm 106:43-44).

Paul writes of the purpose of such patience: “Or do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4).
passages.asks: The people did not leave the LORD in one great act. They drifted toward gods that seemed to promise rain and harvests. Ask what you trust to keep you safe and fed that quietly competes with God. Then look at verse 18. Ask whether you believe that God is moved by your distress even when it is your own fault, and what that kindness is meant to lead you to.

passages.happening:
The anger of the LORD burns again, and he gives his reason. Israel has broken the covenant he laid down for their fathers and has not listened to his voice (verse 20). “I will no longer drive out before them any of the nations Joshua left when he died” (verse 21).

There is a second reason as well. “In this way I will test whether Israel will keep the way of the LORD by walking in it as their fathers did” (verse 22).

That, the writer says, is why the LORD left those nations in place and did not hand them all to Joshua at once (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends by answering a question chapter 1 raised. Why were so many Canaanite towns still standing? The answer has two sides.

The first is judgment. Israel had made agreements with the peoples of the land and had not torn down their altars. So God gives Israel what it chose. The nations stay, and their gods with them.

The second is a test. Living among other peoples and their gods would show what Israel really was, whether it would keep the LORD's way or not. The next chapter adds one more purpose: it taught a new generation, which had never known war, how to fight.

A covenant is a binding relationship with promises and duties on both sides. Israel had sworn at Shechem to serve the LORD. Now it had broken that promise, and the warnings the covenant contained were coming true.
passages.later:
Joshua had said what would follow if Israel broke the covenant: “then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and you will quickly perish from this good land He has given you” (Joshua 23:16).

The opening verses of the next chapter name the nations that were left: “These nations were left to test the Israelites, to find out whether they would keep the commandments of the LORD, which He had given their fathers through Moses” (Judges 3:4). The law had used the same language of testing in the wilderness, where God led Israel forty years ‘to know what was in your heart’ (Deuteronomy 8:2).
passages.hard:
If God could have driven out the nations, why did he leave them to test and to punish Israel?

The chapter gives two reasons that sit together. The nations remain as judgment, because Israel made covenants with them and did not tear down their altars (verses 2-3 and 20-21). And they remain as a test, to show whether Israel would keep the LORD's way (verse 22).

Some readers find it troubling that God would leave his people in a place where they were likely to fail. Others see in it the seriousness of a covenant. God does not force faithfulness on anyone. He lets his people face what their choices bring, and he still comes to rescue them, again and again.

The chapter holds God's justice and his mercy side by side, and it does not resolve every tension between them. Neither should a reader in a hurry.
passages.asks: God let Israel live with the results of its choices, and he did not stop loving them. Ask what choices in your own past still shape your life, and whether you have treated them as a test or only as a burden. And ask what it would look like to keep the LORD's way in the middle of the very things that have pulled you away from it.
